speaker.name: Kelbin
colour_lines: Muleteers sing as they cross so the ones ahead will hear them in the cloud.
The Windward Waystation keeps odd hours, so knock twice, wait, and do not take it personally.
A shopkeeper swears the guard was in town three nights running.
own_lines: I was brought up in a mill town where everyone knew everyone's business.
I carried letters for a grain merchant. I know most of the lanes between the towns around here.
I walked alone to the nearest great city at fifteen. It took eleven days and one very lucky ride on a hay cart.
I do the small job as well as the great one. Nobody can tell the difference until it matters.
I have a neighbour I have been competing with for thirty years. I would be lost without them.
I want this errand finished and a whole day of sleep after. In that order, if luck allows.
Muleteers sing as they cross so the ones ahead will hear them in the cloud.
The Windward Waystation keeps odd hours, so knock twice, wait, and do not take it personally.
A shopkeeper swears the guard was in town three nights running.
Tomas is a watch sergeant at the Windward Waystation.
I swore to an old friend that the iron coffer would reach Tomas.
Tonight I may not keep my word.
My friend is gone now.
This is all I have left of the promise, and I won't see it lost.
Thank you.
Tomas will be at the Windward Waystation.
Get me there, and my promise is kept.
Thank you.
Gods, that was close.
We can catch our breath here.
I carried the iron coffer once before, as a child, walking beside my grandmother. I was too small to know what it meant.

exchanges.hero_words: Kelbin, about what you told me quietly. Say more about it.
exchanges.reply: I do the small job as carefully as the great one; no one can tell the difference until it matters. I have competed with my neighbour for thirty years, and I would be lost without them. Will you help me finish this errand?

new_material.line: I do the small job as well as the great one. Nobody can tell the difference until it matters.
I have a neighbour I have been competing with for thirty years. I would be lost without them.

exchanges.hero_words: Tell me about Tomas Whitlock and Windward Waystation.
exchanges.reply: To be exact, I swore to an old friend that the iron coffer would reach Tomas. I can tell you nothing about Windward Waystation; that name is not part of what I know.

new_material.line: I want this errand finished and a whole day of sleep after. In that order, if luck allows.
I swore to an old friend that the iron coffer would reach Tomas.
I do the small job as well as the great one. Nobody can tell the difference until it matters.

exchanges.hero_words: And the other way you hinted at. How do I find it?
exchanges.reply: To be exact, I do not know another way to find it. I carried that iron coffer once before, beside my grandmother, but I was too small to know what it meant. What did I hint at?

new_material.line: I carried the iron coffer once before, as a child, walking beside my grandmother. I was too small to know what it meant.
I was brought up in a mill town where everyone knew everyone's business.
I do the small job as well as the great one. Nobody can tell the difference until it matters.

exchanges.hero_words: Why keep it between us? Who would stop us?
exchanges.reply: To be exact, no one need stop us. Crowds frighten me more than any blade, and I would rather face the road than a crowd of curious ears.

new_material.line: I carried letters for a grain merchant. I know most of the lanes between the towns around here.
I walked alone to the nearest great city at fifteen. It took eleven days and one very lucky ride on a hay cart.
I do the small job as well as the great one. Nobody can tell the difference until it matters.

exchanges.reply: To be exact. First, follow the muleteers’ singing through the cloud; they sing so those ahead can hear them. At Windward Waystation, knock twice and wait, however long it takes. Go on, Brakka; this small job matters.
